title: Why Coaching Taught Me to Stop Solving
author: Rod Naquin
summary: A veteran teacher describes how coaching a student teacher for a second consecutive semester forced him to abandon his instinct toward offering quick fixes, since each solution (cold-call more, slow the pacing, give clearer directions) reliably surfaced a new problem a week later that the fix itself had quietly caused. He rebuilds his coaching approach around two research frameworks: Mary Kennedy's argument that teaching is organized around five permanent, competing tensions (portraying curriculum content, enlisting participation, exposing student thinking, containing behavior, and accommodating the teacher's own needs) that can never be solved, only managed in trade-offs across an entire career, and Adam Lefstein's argument that classroom dialogue itself should be treated as an unresolvable problem full of competing tensions rather than an achievable ideal state. Combining the two, Kennedy identifies which of the five permanent tensions is live in a given moment, while Lefstein supplies the lens for examining how that tension plays out specifically through classroom talk. The practical result is a two-step coaching cycle: first naming which Kennedy problem is the current growth edge, then using Lefstein's framework to identify the specific trade-off the student teacher navigated, often unconsciously, during a discussion. The piece closes with a concrete 'name the trade-off' coaching move, contrasting generic advice ('cold-call more') with trade-off-naming feedback that hands the choice back to the person being coached with the actual cost made visible.
points: Reframes teaching problems as five permanent, competing tensions (per Mary Kennedy) rather than solvable issues: portraying curriculum content, enlisting participation, exposing student thinking, containing behavior, and accommodating the teacher's own needs, managed in trade-offs for an entire career.

Adopts Adam Lefstein's argument that classroom dialogue itself should be treated as a problem full of real tensions rather than an achievable ideal, rejecting the common framing that positions non-dialogic classroom talk as simply a flaw to be trained away.

Describes a specific realization that drove the reframe: repeatedly offering quick-fix coaching advice (cold-call more, slow the pacing) reliably produced a new problem a week later that the fix itself had quietly caused.

Combines the two frameworks into a concrete two-step coaching cycle: first identify which of Kennedy's five tensions is the live growth edge, then use Lefstein's lens to name the specific trade-off playing out through classroom talk in that moment.

Supplies a specific, reusable coaching script that replaces prescriptive advice ('you should cold-call more') with trade-off-naming feedback that names the competing costs explicitly and hands the decision back to the person being coached.
quotes: Early on, I noticed myself defaulting to solutions. Try cold-calling. Slow down the pacing. Give clearer directions. Each one landed fine in the moment, but a week later a new problem would surface, often one my 'solution' had quietly caused.

Portraying curriculum content, presenting ideas accurately without oversimplifying them into meaninglessness. Enlisting student participation, getting kids to engage without losing the thread of the lesson. Containing student behavior, keeping order without shutting down the very risk-taking that learning requires.

The trick, and the part that took me a while to internalize, is that these problems compete with each other. Push harder on participation and you may lose your grip on behavior. There's no clean sequence where you check off 'curriculum' and move to 'participation.'
Kennedy tells me which problem is showing up. Lefstein gives me a lens to look inside that problem when it's happening through talk, which, in an English classroom, is most of the time.

Not: 'You should cold-call more to get more voices in.' Instead: 'It sounds like calling on more kids might get you wider participation, but it might cost you the safety some of these students need to be wrong out loud. Which matters more to you right now, for this class?'
